INDIVIDUAL SPECIES GUIDE · NOT A STOCK LISTING

Galah Cockatoo

The Galah, also called the rose-breasted cockatoo, is a recognisable pink-and-grey Australian parrot. It is lively and sociable, but its need for interaction, activity and a thoughtful routine is much greater than its moderate size suggests.

Scientific nameEolophus roseicapilla
Typical adult sizeAbout 35 cm long; commonly around 270–350 g, with individual variation.
Lifetime planningCan live for many decades; use a long-term care plan rather than a guaranteed figure.

Overview and appearance

Galahs have a rose-pink face and chest, pale pink crest, grey back and wings, and a lighter underside to the wings. They are a medium-sized cockatoo with a mobile crest and strong bill. In Australia, the species is also known as the rose-breasted cockatoo and occupies a range of open habitats.

The playful impression made by a Galah should not obscure that it is a cockatoo: an intelligent, vocal bird with social needs and a powerful beak. A companion needs safe opportunities to climb, chew and forage, plus an environment that accommodates powder down and regular cleaning.

Personality and social needs

Galahs are often active, curious and engaging, although individual confidence and preferred contact differ. They may seek attention and can become demanding if their day offers little to do. Set a predictable rhythm with interaction, independent play, rest and foraging rather than relying on continuous handling.

Positive, calm contact should respect the bird’s choices. Household members can learn consistent cues and boundaries, while children should only interact under close adult supervision. A safe retreat lets a Galah move away from noise and activity when it needs a pause.

Typical adult size

At about 35 cm long and commonly around 270–350 g, a Galah is smaller than many cockatoos but remains sturdy and active. A suitable enclosure should allow climbing, wing stretching and movement between perches. Plan safe supervised time outside it, not just a compact cage because the bird is not macaw-sized.

Expected lifespan and long-term care

Galahs may live for many decades. Published estimates differ and an individual’s life cannot be predicted from a general range. Long-term plans should account for changing household circumstances, ongoing care and who could take responsibility if needed.

Talking and vocalisation

Galahs communicate with calls, whistles and sometimes learned sounds. A cockatoo’s voice can be penetrating, and no training plan can guarantee a quiet bird. Consider the sound levels acceptable to everyone at home and neighbours, particularly if the bird will spend time alone during the day.

Intelligence and reward-based training

Their curiosity supports reward-based training and enrichment. Practise simple skills such as target following, stepping onto a perch and settling at a station, using brief sessions. Foraging materials and safe objects to manipulate help channel activity. Avoid encouraging rough play with hands or reinforcing unsafe behaviours.

Diet and nutrition

Offer suitable formulated food alongside a wide variety of fresh vegetables, with fruit and calorie-dense treats measured thoughtfully. A seed-heavy menu is not automatically balanced. Ask an avian veterinarian to consider the individual bird’s established diet and condition, and seek advice before making substantial changes or adding supplements.

Housing, exercise and enrichment

Provide a secure, appropriately sized enclosure, varied perches and daily supervised movement in a bird-safe space. Cockatoos enjoy shredding and manipulating safe materials, so rotate enrichment and inspect it for damage. Galahs may produce powder down; consider room ventilation, cleaning and the household environment when planning.

Suitability and questions to ask

A Galah may suit an engaged household ready for regular interaction, noise, cleaning and a long-lived companion. Smaller size does not make a cockatoo an easy starter pet. Consider whether the household can offer activity while also teaching the bird to settle and occupy itself safely.

Before enquiring, ask about a particular bird’s age, daily routine, diet, social behaviour and handling preferences. Discuss how to prepare its enclosure and home, and confirm whether an individual Galah is currently available. Species descriptions are educational and cannot confirm stock.
